newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin goes to hospital with signs of pneumonia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin goes to hospital with signs of pneumonia.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was taken to hospital on Wednesday with first signs of pneumonia, raising new fears about his health two months after heart surgery.
The Kremlin said doctors had ordered the 65-year-old president back to the Central Clinical Hospital in Moscow where he recuperated after his quintuple bypass on November 5.

The president, who had been looking pale and tired, had already cancelled all appointments since Monday because of what the Kremlin said was a heavy cold. Doctors said the cold was not related to the operation and did not threaten his heart.
"Doctors have stated that the first signs of pneumonia developing have appeared," a Kremlin statement said.
"In connection with this, in order to make a better diagnosis and to conduct appropriate treatment, a decision has been taken to take him to the Central Clinical Hospital for several days."

A Kremlin spokesman confirmed Yeltsin was in hospital but gave no other details. He did not mention the trigger which controls Russia's nuclear arsenal but it usually accompanies Yeltsin at all times.
Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks in 1995 and spent much of last year out of the Kremlin with health problems, had been resting at a country residence outside Moscow because of his illness.

Renat Akchurin, who led the team that operated on Yeltsin's heart, had told Itar-Tass news agency earlier on Wednesday that it would be "pure speculation" to suggest the cold was related to the bypass operation or was a threat to his heart.
Russian doctors did not immediately say how serious pneumonia, a potentially fatal inflammation of the lungs, would be to a patient just two months after heart surgery.

Foreign experts, offering initial impressions, told Reuters the pneumonia was probably not related to Yeltsin's heart problems and surgery. They said there was a good chance of recovery if the disease was treated quickly.
"Unsually in people who have pneumonia, it's not an unusually high-risk situation," said Dr Richard Katz, a cardiologist at the George Washington University medical school.

The president returned to work in the Kremlin on December 23. He had been holding regular meetings since then, including having talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl last Saturday, at which the Kremlin leader looked pale and ill at ease.
His last announced meetings were on Monday, when he discussed relations with NATO with top Russian leaders and security officials and held a separate meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Under the constitution, Chernomyrdin would stand in for up to three months before a new election if Yeltsin proved unable to govern. He stepped in for about a day when the Kremlin leader had his bypass but Yeltsin quickly took back his powers when he came round after the surgery.
The 58-year-old prime minister, a loyal Yeltsin ally, had been due to start a brief leave on Wednesday but it was not clear if he had left Moscow.
Yeltsin's absence fuelled a struggle for position among Kremlin officials that culminated in the October sacking of security adviser Alexander Lebed amid charges of coup plots.
Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov is supervising the medical team treating the president.
Akchurin said that although, in the two or three months after surgery, "it is better to avoid any illness, the president's cold can scarcely cause problems for the heart".
Yeltsins press secretary said on Monday the president had a "heavy cold" and a temperature of 37.5 degrees Celsius (99.5 Fahrenheit) but that it had nothing to do with his heart.
Russian media said several of the president's family, including his younger grandson Gleb and his wife Naina, had fallen victim to a flue epidemic sweeping Moscow over New Year.
Veteran Texan heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who advised Akchurin during the heart surgery, told Reuters on Monday the president was recovering on schedule.

"Based on the reports I'm getting, it would appear his cardiac function has been virtually restored to normal," DeBakey said. He said he did not think the president's return to work had contributed to his catching cold.
